Only a heading, 'pro 9 (unicum)', and a figure are on this page. There is no computation. The figure is a large array of small pencil circles on squared paper, covering the whole width of the sheet, which has a vertical fold near x≈655 px. A square, about 8 grid cells on a side, is outlined in the left-centre around one block of the array.

What the figure shows (my measurements from the image, approximate):
(a) Every grid row carries points, and the rows are spaced exactly one grid cell apart (about 22.7 px).
(b) Within a row, the points recur every 8 cells (about 185 px). Down a column the pattern also recurs every 8 rows (rows at y≈179 and y≈362 have points at x≈239, 425, 607, 792). So the drawing is a doubly periodic tiling of the plane by one block, with one point per row and per column in each block.
(c) Reading one period, with row r = 0..7 counted from the top (y≈179) and column c measured from x≈100, the occupied columns look like (6,2,1,5,3,0,4,7). This reading is uncertain.
(d) The outlined square appears to be one fundamental block of this tiling.

The heading points to the n-queens problem with n = 9. 'Unicum' means 'the unique one': presumably the unique arrangement, up to symmetry, with some special property for n = 9. Two things support this:
- The next leaf (fol. 49v/50) shows twelve 8×8 boards with eight dots each, one per row and column. These are evidently the 12 essentially distinct solutions of the eight-queens problem, with cross-references such as '5 (4,6)' and '12 (8,6)'.
- Gauss's 1850 correspondence with Schumacher on the queens problem.

Repeating a board periodically over the plane is the natural way to study 'regular' or toroidal (modular) solutions. In a toroidal solution the queens sit at c ≡ a·r + b (mod n), and the periodic picture lets one see at a glance which diagonals are hit.

What I cannot settle from the image (my inference, flagged as such):
- The precise property that makes the n = 9 pattern a 'unicum'.
- Whether the period really is 8 cells, or 9 lattice lines counted inclusively. The outlined box spans about 8 cells, i.e. 9 grid lines.
- With my reading, the block is not a valid queens arrangement: rows 1 and 2 hold points at columns 2 and 1, which are diagonal neighbours. Either my column reading is off by a cell, the figure is a deliberate study of a non-modular or reflected arrangement, or the figure concerns a related placement problem. No toroidal 9-queens solution exists, since gcd(9,6) ≠ 1. So any 9-periodic picture must contain diagonal coincidences somewhere in the plane, which may be exactly what Gauss was examining.

This is most likely a measurement/reading uncertainty on my part, or a deliberately 'bad' pattern, rather than a slip by Gauss.

results.what: Doubly periodic (tiled) drawing of a one-point-per-row-and-column arrangement, headed 'for 9 (unique)'; context is the n-queens problem (following leaf lists the 12 fundamental 8-queens solutions).
results.modern_name: n-queens problem; periodic/toroidal (modular) queen placements; classification of solutions up to the dihedral symmetry group
results.usually_credited_to: Eight queens: Max Bezzel (1848), Franz Nauck (1850, all 92 solutions). Toroidal/modular solutions exist iff gcd(n,6)=1: Pólya (1918). Systematic n-queens counts: Günther, Glaisher (1874), later authors.

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's interest in the queens problem in 1850 (letters to Schumacher) is well documented, as is the history of his attempts at counting (Campbell 1977). This sheet is a figure-only working note: apparently a periodic tiling used to study 9×9 arrangements. It adds a minor unpublished detail, his use of periodic plane tilings and attention to n = 9. If it showed he grasped the toroidal criterion gcd(n,6)=1 before Pólya, that would be more notable, but nothing on the page establishes this.
